kernelIdea: Proving ¬q ⇒ ¬p proves p ⇒ q. Choose it when the hypothesis you are handed is awkward to compute with.

kernels.l1: Sometimes the easy way to check a promise is to check it backwards.
kernels.l2: You can show a promise is kept by flipping it around the good way first, and then showing the flipped one is kept.
kernels.l3: Because a claim and its contrapositive are always worth the same, you may prove the contrapositive instead. Do that when the if part you were handed is hard to work with.
kernels.l4: Since p ⇒ q ≡ ¬q ⇒ ¬p, proving the contrapositive proves the original. Choose it when the hypothesis p is negative or awkward and ¬q is easier to compute with.
kernels.l5: Proof by contrapositive replaces the goal p ⇒ q with the equivalent goal ¬q ⇒ ¬p, and is the method of choice when ¬q is more usable than p.
kernels.l6: A proof by contrapositive announces the switch, proves ¬q ⇒ ¬p directly, and invokes the equivalence to conclude p ⇒ q.
kernels.l7: Proof by contrapositive establishes p ⇒ q by proving the logically equivalent ¬q ⇒ ¬p; it is indicated when the hypothesis is a negation or concerns a composite quantity that the conclusion's negation decomposes.
kernels.l8: Contrapositive proof is a change of goal along a logical equivalence; it differs from proof by contradiction in that it assumes only ¬q, not ¬q together with p, and so remains available in weaker logics.
